newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian cattle drown in shipwreck off Guam.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian cattle drown in shipwreck off Guam.

text.p: Almost 1,600 head of Australian cattle en route to Japan have drowned in a shipwreck 60 km southwest of Guam, a spokesman for the Australian Meat and Livestock Corp (AMLC) said.
This is the first loss of Australian cattle at sea and follows the drowning of almost 70,000 Australian sheep when a burning ship sunk off the Seychelles in September.
The drowned steers were on board the Guernsey Express and sailing from Brisbane to Japan.
The ship went down in typhoon Dale, south west of Guam, at about midnight local time on Saturday.
"I think it's safe to say they've drowned," Australian Meat and Livestock Corp (AMLC) spokesman Chris Rowley told Reuters.
The shipment of 1,600 head was an average-sized shipment and bound for Osaka, he said.
All crew from the vessel were safe, he said.
The vessel went down in very heavy seas with 100 km per hour-plus winds, he said.
"It's a very unfortunate, a regrettable, first," Rowley said.

What appeared to occur was that a couple of crew members sustained injuries in the peak period of the storm and were in the process of being transferred to Guam hospital when the ship began taking on water and went down, he said.
Further details were not presently to hand, he said.
According to early reports, some cattle escaped the ship and initially floated near were the vessel went down.
The loss of the 1,600 head of cattle quickly intensified calls for the banning of Australia's growing live animal trade.

Mark Pearson, president of animal welfare group Animal Liberation, the most active opponent of the live export industry, told Reuters the drowning of the cattle reconfirmed his group's stand against "this barbaric trade".
"I want to end the live cattle trade and the live sheep trade. Enough is enough," said Richard Jones of Animal Liberation.
A campaign was about to be launched in conjunction with London-based International Fund for Animal Welfare, with its 1.5 million members world-wide, to end the trade, he said.
Pearson said the loss of almost 70,000 sheep aboard the Uniceb in September involved sheep being burned alive.
The 14,990 tonne Uniceb caught fire then sank off the Seychelles in the Indian Ocean after crew abandoned ship leaving 67,000 live sheep aboard the blazing vessel.
Live cattle exports from the state of Queensland increased by 53 percent to 554,352 head in booming trade in the latest year to September.
Australia's total live cattle exports in 1996/97 to June 30 were recently projected by the New South Wales Farmers' Association to reach 750,000 head, up from 633,000 in 1995/96.
The booming trade, fuelled by high slaughter and processing costs in Australia, has recently led to questions in the livestock trade of whether animals might be slaughtered at sea.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
